current_example.title: Example: Identifying True Statements About Bases of Abstract Vector Spaces

q-107132.name: Question 1
q-107132.problem:
Consider the vector space ${R}_{3}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $3.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${R}_{3}[t]$

II. $3t-2{t}^{3}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}\}$

III. $\{t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}\}$ is a basis of ${R}_{3}[t]$
q-107132.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation 

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot t+{x}_{2}\cdot {t}^{2}+{x}_{3}\cdot {t}^{3}=0,
$$

 
is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
3t-2{t}^{3}=3\cdot t+0\cdot {t}^{2}+(-2)\cdot {t}^{3}.
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the polynomial $1+t$ can't be written as a linear combination of the set
$\{t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}\}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

  2. 3t−2t3 can be expressed as a linear combination of {t,t2,t3}

Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation x1⋅t+x2⋅t2+x3⋅t3=0, is true if and only if x1=x2=x3=0. So, the set is linearly independent.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, 3t−2t3=3⋅t+0⋅t2+(−2)⋅t3.

  • Statement III is false. For example, the polynomial 1+t can't be written as a linear combination of the set
    {t,t2,t3}.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

q-36308.name: Question 2
q-36308.problem:
Consider the vector space ${R}_{2}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $2.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{0,t,{t}^{2}\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${R}_{2}[t]$

II. ${t}^{2}-2t$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{0,t,{t}^{2}\}$

III. $\{0,t,{t}^{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}_{2}[t]$
q-36308.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Notice that 

$$
1\cdot 0+0\cdot t+0\cdot {t}^{2}=0,
$$

 
where the first coefficient is nonzero, so the set is linearly dependent. In general, any set that contains a zero-vector is linearly dependent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
{t}^{2}-2t=0\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot t+1\cdot {t}^{2}.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the set is not linearly independent, it can't form a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

q-107127.name: Question 3
q-107127.problem:
Consider the vector space ${R}_{2}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $2.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{1,t,t+1\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${R}_{2}[t]$

II. $2t+1$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{1,t,t+1\}$

III. $\{1,t,t+1\}$ is a basis of ${R}_{2}[t]$
q-107127.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Notice that 

$$
1\cdot 1+1\cdot t+(-1)\cdot (t+1)=0,
$$

 
where all three coefficients are nonzero, so the set is linearly dependent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
2t+1=0\cdot 1+1\cdot t+1\cdot (t+1).
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the set is not linearly independent, it can't form a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

q-107130.name: Question 4
q-107130.problem:
Consider the vector space ${R}_{2}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $2.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{2,{t}^{2}\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${R}_{2}[t]$

II. $2+{t}^{2}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{2,{t}^{2}\}$

III. $\{2,{t}^{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}_{2}[t]$
q-107130.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation 

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot 2+{x}_{2}\cdot {t}^{2}=0,
$$

 
is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
2+{t}^{2}=1\cdot 2+1\cdot {t}^{2}.
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the polynomial $t$ can't be written as a linear combination of

$$
\{2,{t}^{2}\}
$$

since all these combinations result in polynomials without terms of the form $at.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

q-94870.name: Question 6
q-94870.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
q-94870.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{4}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}={x}_{4}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}]=2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+8\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the set is linearly independent and for any matrix in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R),$ we get 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]=a\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+b\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+c\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+d\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, [2−583]=2⋅[1000]+(−5)⋅[0100]+8⋅[0010]+3⋅[0001].

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, the set is linearly independent and for any matrix in M2(R), we get [abcd]=a⋅[1000]+b⋅[0100]+c⋅[0010]+d⋅[0001].

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

q-36571.name: Question 7
q-36571.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
q-36571.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]=-2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+5\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of 

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}
$$

since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{12}=0:$

$$
a\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+b\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

q-94865.name: Question 8
q-94865.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
q-94865.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is false. Notice that all linear combinations of 

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}
$$

result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{21}=0.$

- Statement III is false. Since the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of the set, it can't form a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

q-107535.name: Question 9
q-107535.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
q-107535.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ So the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]=2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+0\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of 

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\}
$$

since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{11}={a}_{22}:$

$$
a\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+b\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+c\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & a\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

q-94869.name: Question 10
q-94869.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
q-94869.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Notice that

$$
0\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+1\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]+1\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

where some coefficients are nonzero, so the set is linearly dependent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]=(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+0\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]+2\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

q-36478.name: Question 11
q-36478.problem:
Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}+{b}_{3},{b}_{3}\}$ is a basis of $V$

II. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\}$ is linearly independent

III. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $V$
q-36478.worked_solution:
Since $B$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $B$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}({b}_{2}+{b}_{3})+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}){b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}+{b}_{3},{b}_{3}\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}+{b}_{3},{b}_{3}\}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}({b}_{2}+{b}_{3})+({x}_{3}-{x}_{2}){b}_{3}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since ${b}_{1}+{b}_{2}$ is a linear combination of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$, the given set is linearly dependent.

- Statement III is false since the vector ${b}_{3}$ can't be written as a linear combination of $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\}.$ But then

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{3} & ={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}({b}_{1}+{b}_{2}) \\  & =({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which would mean that $B$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $B$ is a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$

II. $\{{b}_{1},2{b}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$

III. $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$
q-107537.worked_solution:
Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. The set $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{2}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}(2{b}_{2}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+(2{x}_{2}){b}_{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\{{b}_{1},2{b}_{2}\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{{b}_{1},2{b}_{2}\}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}{b}_{2}
$$

- Statement III is false. The set $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the third vector is a linear combination of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ This means that the set is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

q-80631.problem:

II. $\{-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$

III. $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$
q-80631.worked_solution:
Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. The set $\{x,{b}_{2},{c}_{1}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(-2{b}_{3})+{x}_{2}(3{b}_{1})+{x}_{3}(5{b}_{2}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2{x}_{1}){b}_{3}+(3{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+(5{x}_{3}){b}_{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}=0 \\ 3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\{-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}\}:$

$$

$$

- Statement III is false. Since $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$, any vector of ${R}^{2},$ including the given vector $x,$ can be written as a linear combination of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ This means that $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x\}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

q-36309.name: Question 14
q-36309.problem:
Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ is linearly independent

II. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3},w\}$ is linearly independent

III. $\{2{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is a basis of $V$
q-36309.worked_solution:
Since $B$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $B$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, if $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}=0,
$$

where at least one of $x$'s is not zero. But then 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+0{b}_{3}=0,
$$

which would mean that $B$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $B$ is a basis.

- Statement II is false. Since $B$ is a basis of $V,$ it is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors. This means that if we add any new vector to the set, it becomes linearly dependent.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(2{b}_{1})+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{x}_{1}){b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\{2{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{2{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}(2{b}_{1})+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent

II. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3},w\}$ is a basis of $V$

III. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{1}+{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent
q-107938.worked_solution:
Since $B$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $B$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, if $\{{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{2}+{x}_{2}{b}_{3}=0,
$$

where at least one of $x$'s is not zero. But then 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+0{b}_{3}=0,
$$

which would mean that $B$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $B$ is a basis.

- Statement II is false. Since $B$ is a basis of $V,$ it is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors. This means that if we add any new vector to the set, it becomes linearly dependent. Hence, the given set is not a basis for $V.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}({b}_{1}+{b}_{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}){b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."
